3010:
Coincident means "occupying the same point in time or space." When two things are coincident, they line up — either they happen at the same moment, exist at the same location, or match each other in some meaningful way.

Think of it as two separate things landing on exactly the same spot — whether that spot is a moment in time, a position in space, or a point of agreement.

1. Happening at the same time

This is the most common meaning. Two events are coincident when they occur during the same period or at the same moment.

"The economic crisis was coincident with the drought — both hit the country in the same year."

"The power cut was coincident with the start of the match."

Notice: it simply states they happened together. It doesn't say why or whether it was surprising. That's important (more on this below).

2. Occupying the same position in space (especially in geometry)

In mathematics and geometry, two lines, points, or shapes are coincident when they lie exactly on top of each other — they share every single point.

Imagine drawing a line on paper, then drawing another line directly over it so perfectly that you can't tell them apart. Those two lines are coincident — they are not just parallel, they are identical in position.

"When you solve a system of two linear equations and both equations turn out to be the same line, the lines are coincident — they have infinitely many solutions."

This meaning is precise and technical, but it follows the same logic: two things occupying the exact same spot.

3. In agreement or correspondence with something

Two things are coincident when they align, match, or correspond — when one fits neatly with the other.

"Her ambitions were coincident with the organization's goals — she was a natural fit."

"His observations were coincident with what the data showed."

Here, "coincident" means the two things are in harmony, pointing in the same direction.

In real usage, "coincident with" is the most natural construction. The word rarely stands alone without a "with" following it.

✅ "The launch was coincident with the anniversary of the company."
✅ "The flooding was coincident with the high tide."
✅ "His rise to power was coincident with a period of public unrest."

This is where most learners go wrong, so pay close attention.

These two words look related, and they are — but they carry very different meanings.

Coincidental means something happened by chance — it was unexpected, surprising, or accidental. It carries the sense of "what a strange accident!"

"It was coincidental that we both showed up wearing the same shirt — neither of us planned it."

Coincident is neutral. It simply states that two things happened at the same time or in the same place. It says nothing about whether this was surprising, planned, or accidental.

"The two meetings were coincident — they were both scheduled for 3 p.m." (Just a fact. No judgment.)

The test: Ask yourself — does the sentence need to imply chance or surprise? If yes, use coincidental. If you're just stating a neutral fact about timing, position, or correspondence, use coincident.
Register and where you'll encounter it

Coincident is a formal word. You will rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. Instead, you'll encounter it in:

  • Academic writing ("The peak in crime rates was coincident with the period of unemployment.")
  • Scientific and research papers ("The rise in temperature was coincident with increased solar activity.")
  • Formal reports and journalism ("The policy change was coincident with the minister's resignation.")
  • Mathematics and geometry textbooks ("The two planes are coincident.")

In casual speech, people tend to say "at the same time," "overlapping," or "matching" rather than "coincident." So if you use this word, you're signaling a formal, precise register.
Putting it all together — varied examples

• "The blackout was coincident with the heavy storm — both occurred within the same hour." (timing)
  • "In the solution, the two equations yield coincident lines, meaning any point on one satisfies the other." (geometry)
  • "The CEO's resignation was coincident with the board's announcement of a new strategy." (timing, formal context)
  • "Her research findings were largely coincident with the earlier study published in 2019." (correspondence/agreement)
  • "The festival falls on a date coincident with the harvest season." (timing)

Coincident = two things landing on the exact same spot — in time, in space, or in meaning. No surprise implied, no accident assumed. Just alignment.

Once you have that image — two things landing precisely on the same point — all three meanings click naturally into place.
3011: Something is coincidental when two or more events happen together, around the same time, or in a strikingly similar way — but purely by chance. No one planned it, no one caused it, and one event did not lead to the other. They just happened to line up, and that's it.
Breaking It Down with an Example

Imagine you're sitting at home thinking about an old friend you haven't spoken to in two years. Right at that moment, your phone rings — and it's them.

That is coincidental.

Two things happened at the same time (you thinking of them; them calling you) that seem connected, but there is no real connection. Your thinking didn't make them call. Their calling didn't cause you to think of them. It's pure, random chance that both things happened together.
The Three Things That Make Something Coincidental

For something to be called coincidental, three conditions are usually at work:

  1. Multiple events — there are at least two things happening.
  2. An apparent connection — they seem related, similar, or oddly timed.
  3. No actual link — there's no cause, no plan, no intention tying them together.

If even one of those is missing, the word doesn't quite apply. For instance, if someone planned for two things to happen at the same time, that's intentional — not coincidental.
More Examples to Solidify the Idea

• You and a stranger show up to a party wearing the exact same outfit. Coincidental — neither of you knew what the other would wear.
  • Two scientists on opposite sides of the world publish the same theory on the same day, having never communicated. Coincidental — they arrived at the same idea independently.
  • You mention a word you rarely use, and your friend says, "I literally just read that word five minutes ago." Coincidental — the timing lines up for no particular reason.
  • A detective finds the suspect near the crime scene. The suspect says it's coincidental. That means: "I happened to be there — I had nothing to do with the crime."

This is important to get sharp on:

  • Not the same as "caused." If one event directly leads to another, that's a cause-and-effect relationship, not a coincidence. If you push someone and they fall, that's not coincidental — you caused it.
  • Not the same as "planned" or "intentional." If someone arranges for two things to happen at the same time, it's deliberate. Coincidental is the opposite — no arrangement, no plan.
  • Not the same as "impossible" or "fake." Coincidences genuinely happen. Calling something coincidental doesn't mean it didn't occur or that someone is lying. It just means there's no hidden cause or design behind it.

Here's something worth understanding: coincidences feel striking because the human mind is wired to look for patterns and meaning. When two unrelated things line up in an odd way, it feels significant — it grabs our attention and makes us ask, "How is that possible?"

But saying something is coincidental is a way of saying: "Yes, this looks meaningful — but it's not. It's random chance."

This is why the word often appears in situations where someone might suspect a deeper reason:

"His resignation right after the scandal? That's not coincidental."

The speaker is rejecting the idea that it's coincidence. Flip it around:

"His resignation right after the scandal was entirely coincidental."

Now the speaker is insisting there's no connection — it just happened to look that way.
How It's Used in Real Sentences

• "Their meeting was coincidental — neither of them knew the other would be there."
  • "The two companies launched the same product on the same day. The timing was purely coincidental."
  • "We have the same last name, but we're not related. It's coincidental."
  • "The resemblance between the two paintings is coincidental — the artists never knew each other."

These all belong to the same word family and are worth knowing:

  • Coincidence (noun) — the event or fact itself. "What a coincidence!"
  • Coincide (verb) — when two things happen at the same time or match up. "Their arrival times coincided."
  • Coincidentally (adverb) — used to describe how something happened. "Coincidentally, we both ordered the same dish."
  • Coincidental (adjective) — describes the nature of something as being a coincidence. "The similarity was coincidental."

"Coincidental" describes something that looks like it has a connection but doesn't. This is what separates it from something that's merely random. A lottery ball landing on a number is random, but we wouldn't call it coincidental unless something else lined up with it — say, it matched your birth date exactly.

The word only really comes alive when there's that tension between apparent connection and actual absence of connection.

Coincidental = two or more things happening together or similarly, but only by chance — with no cause, no plan, and no real link between them.

The word is used to describe that eerie, surprising overlap and to clarify (or argue) that it means nothing beyond chance.
3012: A colander is a bowl-shaped kitchen tool full of small holes. You use it to drain liquid away from food. Think of it as a strainer or a sieve built in the shape of a bowl.

Picture a large bowl — but instead of a solid bottom and sides, the entire surface is covered with dozens of small holes. It usually has two handles on the sides (so you can grip it safely) and small feet or a base at the bottom (so it can stand on its own in a sink without tipping over). It's typically made of stainless steel, plastic, or enamel-coated metal.
How it works and what it does

The job of a colander is simple: let liquid pass through while keeping solid food inside.

You hold it over a sink (or set it in the sink), pour your food into it, and the water or liquid drains away through the holes while your food stays in the bowl. The holes are big enough for water to escape, but small enough to catch your food.

• Draining pasta — This is the most classic use. After you boil spaghetti or noodles, you pour the boiling water and pasta into the colander. The water drains away, and the pasta stays behind.
  • Rinsing vegetables or fruits — You put washed grapes, strawberries, or salad leaves into a colander and run water over them. The water drains out, and the food stays clean inside.
  • Draining canned beans or chickpeas — Opening a tin of chickpeas and tipping it into a colander lets the salty liquid run off while keeping the chickpeas.
  • Draining boiled potatoes, rice, or lentils — Same idea as pasta.
How a colander is different from similar things

Since learners often confuse related tools, here are the key distinctions:

Colander vs. Fine-mesh strainer/sieve:
A fine-mesh strainer has very tiny, tightly woven holes — small enough to catch tea leaves or catch lumps in a sauce. A colander has larger holes, meant for chunky solid foods like pasta or vegetables. If you tried to strain soup stock through a colander, most of the small bits would fall right through. So: colander = large holes = chunky foods; fine-mesh strainer = tiny holes = liquids and fine particles.

Colander vs. Salad spinner:
A salad spinner dries lettuce leaves by spinning them, using centrifugal force. A colander simply lets gravity do the work — liquid falls through the holes on its own. Many salad spinners actually have a colander-like inner basket inside them.

Colanders come in different sizes — small ones for rinsing a handful of strawberries, and large ones for draining a full pot of pasta for a family dinner. In most kitchens, the colander is placed inside the sink when in use, so the drained liquid goes directly down the drain.
One important nuance: it must match the food

Because the holes in a colander are relatively large, it works well only for foods that are bigger than the holes. You would not use a colander to drain rice, small seeds, or lentils through a standard colander — they'd fall through. For very small foods, you'd need a colander with smaller, finer holes (sometimes called a fine colander) or switch to a strainer/sieve instead.

A colander is an essential, everyday kitchen bowl with holes in it, designed purely for one purpose: draining liquid from solid food. Its most iconic use is pouring out a pot of boiled pasta so the water escapes and the pasta remains. It's one of the simplest tools in a kitchen, but almost impossible to cook without.
3013:
A "cold war" is a state of deep hostility and intense rivalry between two countries (or groups) that never breaks out into direct, open fighting. They are enemies — but they don't shoot at each other directly. The conflict stays cold, meaning it never heats up into a real, declared, face-to-face war.

Think of it this way: a hot war is when two sides actually fight each other with weapons, soldiers, and direct combat. A cold war is everything just short of that — the tension, the threats, the competition, the hatred — without the shooting happening between those two sides directly.

The word "cold" here means the absence of direct heat — fire and bloodshed between the two main rivals. It does not mean calm or peaceful. A cold war is brimming with fear, suspicion, and aggression. It is a war in every psychological and strategic sense. It's just that the two enemies choose (or are forced) to express their hostility through indirect means rather than direct combat.
How is a cold war actually fought?

Even without direct fighting, the two sides are constantly trying to weaken, undermine, or overpower each other. They do this through:

  • Proxy wars — Instead of fighting each other, each side arms, trains, and supports a third country or group to fight on their behalf. The two main rivals never face each other directly, but they fuel wars elsewhere in the world, each supporting the opposite side.
  • Espionage and spying — Each side secretly steals the other's information, secrets, military plans, and technology.
  • Propaganda — Each side tries to influence public opinion at home and abroad, making the other side look evil, dangerous, or weak.
  • Arms race — Both sides build up enormous stockpiles of weapons, especially nuclear weapons, to intimidate the other. The goal is to make the enemy too afraid to ever attack first.
  • Economic pressure and sanctions — Cutting off trade, blocking financial ties, and trying to make the other side economically weak.
  • Political interference — Trying to influence elections, governments, and leaders in other countries to be friendly to your side.
  • Space races, technology competitions — Competing to appear more powerful, advanced, and capable in the eyes of the world.

All of these are weapons in a cold war — they're just not bullets.
The original Cold War (capital C, capital W)

When people write "the Cold War" with capital letters, they are referring to a specific historical period: the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union (USSR) from roughly 1947 to 1991. This is the event that gave the phrase its name.

After World War II, the US and the USSR emerged as the two most powerful nations on Earth, but they had deeply opposing ideologies. The US championed capitalism and liberal democracy. The USSR championed communism and one-party rule. Neither trusted the other, and both wanted to spread their way of life across the world.

They never fought each other directly — in part because both sides had nuclear weapons, meaning direct war could have destroyed both countries and much of the world. This kept the conflict "cold." But they competed fiercely in every other way: proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola, and elsewhere; a massive nuclear arms race; a space race; espionage (the CIA vs. the KGB); and ideological propaganda wars.

The Cold War ended in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed from within, leaving the United States as the sole superpower.

Beyond the historical Cold War, "cold war" (lowercase) is used as a general concept to describe any prolonged rivalry or hostile standoff between two parties that stops short of open warfare.

For example:

  • "A cold war between China and the US is simmering over trade and technology."
  • "There's been a quiet cold war between those two departments for years."

In casual or journalistic use, it can even refer to intense personal or organizational rivalries — though this broader usage is informal.
The key characteristics that define a cold war

No matter who the parties are, a cold war has these features:

  1. No direct combat between the two main rivals.
  2. Real and intense hostility — it is a genuine conflict, not mere competition.
  3. Indirect methods — proxy fights, propaganda, subversion, economic pressure.
  4. High stakes — typically involving power, dominance, ideology, or survival.
  5. Long duration — cold wars are usually not brief; they can last decades.
  6. Constant tension — both sides remain perpetually on guard, ready to escalate.

A cold war is a war in spirit, strategy, and consequence — but fought through pressure, fear, and indirection rather than direct combat. The name captures the paradox perfectly: it's a war that refuses to burst into flame, yet never stops burning.
3014: "Cold-blooded" carries two distinct meanings — one scientific, one about human character. Both are widely used. Here is everything you need to know.

When we say an animal is cold-blooded, we mean its body temperature is not controlled from the inside. Instead, its body temperature changes depending on how warm or cold the surrounding environment is.

A snake lying in the hot sun gets warm. The same snake moved into a cold room becomes cold and sluggish. It has no internal "thermostat" of its own. Its body takes on the temperature of wherever it is.

Examples of cold-blooded animals:

  • Snakes, lizards, crocodiles (reptiles)
  • Frogs, salamanders (amphibians)
  • Fish

The opposite is warm-blooded — animals like humans, dogs, and birds, who maintain a stable internal body temperature no matter what the environment is like.

"Reptiles are cold-blooded creatures that rely on sunlight to regulate their body heat."

In this scientific context, "cold-blooded" is completely neutral. It is just a biological fact, with no negative judgment attached.
Meaning 2: The Human/Figurative Sense (the more common usage)

This is where the word gets its real power and weight in everyday language.

When "cold-blooded" is used to describe a person, an action, or a crime, it means:

Done deliberately, without any emotion, guilt, hesitation, or mercy — in a calm and calculated way.

The key ideas packed into this meaning are:

1. No emotion. A cold-blooded person does not feel the normal human feelings — guilt, remorse, sadness, pity — that would stop most people from doing harm. They do terrible things without their heart getting in the way.

2. Deliberate and planned. It is never accidental or impulsive. A cold-blooded act is thought out. The person knew what they were doing and chose to do it calmly.

3. Disturbing calmness. This is what makes it especially unsettling. Most serious cruelty happens in rage or panic. Cold-blooded cruelty happens in a state of calm — and that calm is what makes it feel inhuman.

The Metaphor Behind It

The figurative meaning comes directly from the biological one. We naturally associate warmth with emotion, life, and feeling — think of a warm smile, a warm hug, a warm person. Cold, on the other hand, suggests the absence of those feelings. A cold-blooded animal has no internal warmth. A cold-blooded person, metaphorically, has no emotional warmth — no natural human feelings of compassion or conscience to hold them back.

Common Collocations (words it appears with most often)

  • Cold-blooded murder — a killing done calmly and intentionally, not in a fit of rage or panic
  • Cold-blooded killer — a person who kills without emotional disturbance or remorse
  • Cold-blooded attack — a deliberate, emotionless act of violence
  • Cold-blooded ruthlessness — a calculated, merciless approach to getting what one wants

"The judge called it a cold-blooded murder — planned for weeks and carried out without a single moment of hesitation."

"He was described by witnesses as a cold-blooded killer who showed no emotion even as the verdict was read."

"It was a cold-blooded betrayal — she had smiled at his face every single day while quietly working to destroy him."

Strength of the Word

"Cold-blooded" is a strong word. It is not used lightly. You would not call someone cold-blooded simply for being unfriendly, rude, or selfish. It is reserved for serious cruelty — violence, betrayal, harm — delivered without the normal human emotions that would cause most people to pause, feel guilt, or show mercy.

It is almost always negative in tone. In rare cases, it can be used with a kind of dark admiration (e.g., "a cold-blooded chess player who dismantled his opponents without mercy"), but even then, there is an unsettling edge to it.

What It Does NOT Mean

  • It does not mean a person who is simply quiet, reserved, or introverted.
  • It does not mean someone who is merely unfriendly or cold in a social sense (that would just be "cold" or "aloof").
  • It does not mean acting rashly in anger — that is closer to "hot-blooded" behavior. Cold-blooded is the opposite: calm, not angry.
  • It does not describe every bad or cruel person — only those whose cruelty is marked by an eerie, calculated absence of normal feeling.

Synonyms (Figurative Sense)

Callous, heartless, ruthless, pitiless, merciless, unfeeling, calculating.

Each of these captures a piece of what "cold-blooded" means, but none of them carry the full combination of deliberateness + emotional absence + calm the way "cold-blooded" does. That combination is what makes the word uniquely powerful.

Antonyms (Figurative Sense)

Warm-hearted, compassionate, merciful, humane, passionate.

SenseWhat it means

Biological sense: An animal whose body temperature is controlled by the environment, not internally. Neutral in tone.

Figurative sense: A person or act that is deliberately cruel, emotionless, and calm — with no guilt, hesitation, or mercy. Always serious in weight, almost always negative.

The figurative meaning is far more common in everyday language, and when you see or hear "cold-blooded" used about a person, a crime, or an act — it is always saying the same unsettling thing: this was done with full awareness, without feeling, and without flinching.
3015:
Colic is a noun that refers to a type of severe, cramping pain in the belly (abdomen). What makes colic different from ordinary stomach pain is its distinctive wave-like pattern — the pain builds up sharply, reaches a peak, eases off a little, and then surges back again. This cyclical, gripping quality is what defines it. Think of it like a fist clenching and unclenching deep inside the body, repeatedly and painfully.

The pain comes from hollow organs inside the body — such as the intestines, kidneys, or bile ducts — when they go into involuntary muscular spasms or get blocked. These organs have smooth muscle in their walls that normally contracts gently and rhythmically to move things along. When something disrupts this process, those muscles contract violently and cause the intense, cramping pain we call colic.
The Two Main Worlds Where "Colic" Is Used
The word "colic" is used in two distinct but related contexts: medicine (in humans) and veterinary care (especially in horses). Each is important to understand.

In human medicine, colic is used in two important ways:

A. Infant Colic (the most commonly discussed form)

This is probably the first thing most people think of when they hear the word. Infant colic refers to a condition where an otherwise completely healthy baby cries excessively, intensely, and inconsolably — for no apparent reason that a parent can identify or fix.

Doctors typically define it by the "Rule of Three":

  • Crying for more than 3 hours a day
  • On more than 3 days a week
  • For more than 3 weeks in a row

The baby is not sick, not hungry, not hurt in any obvious way — and yet they scream. The crying often happens at the same time each day (commonly in the late afternoon or evening), the baby may pull its legs up toward its belly, clench its fists, and have a red, strained face. Nothing seems to soothe them. This usually begins when a baby is about 2–3 weeks old, gets worst around 6 weeks of age, and then gradually resolves on its own by the time the baby is 3 to 4 months old.

What causes infant colic? Honestly, the medical community does not know for certain. Several theories exist: trapped intestinal gas, an immature or overly sensitive digestive system, an immature nervous system that makes the baby overstimulated and unable to self-soothe, or gut flora imbalances. The discomfort is real, but the precise mechanism isn't fully established. What is well-established is that colic is not the parent's fault, it does not harm the baby long-term, and it resolves on its own.

B. Colic in Adults (a medical term for specific pain syndromes)

In adult medicine, "colic" is used more precisely to describe wave-like cramping pain caused by blockages or spasms in specific hollow organs. Doctors often pair it with a word that tells you which organ is involved:

  • Renal colic — This is the pain caused when a kidney stone travels from the kidney down the narrow tube (ureter) that leads to the bladder. It is widely described as one of the most intense pains a human being can experience. The pain comes in waves, typically starting in the back or side and radiating down toward the groin.
  • Biliary colic — This refers to pain caused by a gallstone temporarily blocking the bile duct (the tube that carries bile from the gallbladder to the intestine). The pain usually occurs in the upper-right part of the abdomen, often after eating fatty food, and can radiate to the back or shoulder.
  • Intestinal colic — A more general term for cramping gut pain caused by gas buildup, intestinal obstruction, or bowel spasms.

In all these adult cases, the common thread is the same: a hollow organ is being blocked or is cramping, and the result is that characteristic severe, wave-like pain.

In veterinary medicine — particularly for horses — colic is an extremely serious and well-known condition. Equine colic is an umbrella term for any kind of abdominal pain in a horse. It is not a single disease but rather a symptom of many possible problems: gas buildup, intestinal blockages, twisted bowels, or other digestive issues.

A horse with colic may show signs like pawing at the ground, looking back at its flank, lying down and rolling, refusing to eat, or sweating without exertion. Colic is one of the leading causes of death in horses, and even a mild case is treated as a medical emergency because a horse's digestive anatomy makes it especially vulnerable — for example, horses cannot vomit, so gas and blockages can build up catastrophically.
Summary of What "Colic" Means Across All Uses

No matter where you encounter the word, colic always involves:

  1. Severe, cramping pain — not a dull ache, but an intense, gripping quality
  2. A wave-like pattern — it surges and ebbs, rather than staying constant
  3. Origin in a hollow organ — intestines, kidneys, bile ducts, or the digestive tract
  4. Distress and urgency — in every context, colic signals that something needs attention

The word functions as a noun whether you say "the baby has colic," "she was diagnosed with renal colic," or "the horse has colic." In each case, it names this specific kind of painful condition rather than describing it as an adjective would.
How "Colic" Is Used in a Sentence

• "The new parents hadn't slept properly in weeks because their baby had colic."
  • "He was rushed to the emergency room with renal colic — the kidney stone was excruciating."
  • "The veterinarian was called immediately when the horse showed signs of colic."
  • "Biliary colic tends to flare up after rich, fatty meals."

Because infant colic is so common and so distressing, the word "colic" in everyday conversation (outside of a medical or veterinary context) almost always refers to the baby condition. If someone says, "My newborn has colic," you immediately understand: a healthy baby, inconsolable crying, exhausted parents, and a condition that will pass with time. The medical uses (renal colic, biliary colic) are more clinical terms you're more likely to encounter in a doctor's office or hospital setting.
3016: Colicky means relating to, caused by, or affected by colic — a condition involving sharp, cramping pain, usually in the belly. It can describe a person (especially a baby), an animal, or a type of pain.

To understand colicky, you need to understand colic. Colic is not a disease — it is a pattern of severe pain that originates in the hollow organs of the body (the intestines, the stomach, the bile duct, the urinary tract, etc.). What makes colic distinctive is that the pain doesn't stay at the same level. It rises and falls in waves — it grips you intensely, then eases a little, then grips you again. This wave-like, cramping quality is the signature of colic.

The pain is caused by the squeezing and contracting of the muscular walls of hollow organs — for example, when your intestines are trying to push out trapped gas, or when your kidney is trying to pass a stone through the ureter. The organ contracts powerfully, and that contraction is felt as severe, gripping pain.

1. Colicky pain
This is the most precise, medically accurate use of the word. When a doctor describes pain as colicky, they mean it is:

  • Cramping and spasm-like — not a dull ache, but a gripping, squeezing feeling
  • Intermittent — it comes in waves; it intensifies, then briefly lets up, then returns
  • Located in the abdomen or related internal organs (though it can radiate elsewhere)

Examples of colicky pain:

  • The pain from kidney stones passing through the ureter is classically described as colicky — it is one of the most severe pains in medicine, and it comes in waves as the ureter contracts
  • The abdominal pain from trapped gas or a blocked intestine is colicky
  • Gallstone pain (biliary colic) is colicky pain felt in the upper right abdomen

So if a doctor says, "The patient has colicky abdominal pain," they are telling you something very specific: the pain has that characteristic wave-like, cramping nature, which points them toward a particular set of causes.

2. A colicky baby (or infant)
This is the most common everyday use of the word, and it is what most people think of first. A colicky baby is an otherwise healthy infant who cries excessively — intensely, persistently, and for no clear reason that a parent can solve. The baby appears to be in pain: they pull their knees up toward their belly, arch their back, clench their fists, and their face turns red. The crying typically happens in long bouts, often in the evening.

The general medical rule of thumb is: a baby is considered colicky if they cry for more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks, and nothing seems to comfort them.

The precise cause of colic in infants is not fully understood — different theories involve digestive gas, gut immaturity, gut bacteria, overstimulation, or other factors. What we do know is that it is temporary and that most babies grow out of it by around 3–4 months of age.

When you call a baby colicky, you are saying they suffer from infant colic. The word carries a sense of distress, discomfort, and the helplessness a parent feels when they cannot soothe their child.

3. A colicky adult or older person
Less commonly, an adult can also be described as colicky if they are prone to bouts of colic — meaning they suffer from recurring cramping pain in the abdomen. This use is less frequent in everyday speech, but it is grammatically and medically accurate.

4. A colicky horse or animal
Colic is extremely common and serious in horses. A horse that is experiencing or prone to colic is described as colicky. You might hear: "The horse was found colicky in its stall." In veterinary medicine, colic in horses is a major emergency because horses cannot vomit, making intestinal blockages especially dangerous. The term colicky is used widely in equine care.
The single idea behind all uses

Whether it's describing pain, a baby, or an animal, the word colicky always connects back to the same core idea: the character of colic — something involving sharp, gripping, wave-like discomfort in the body, typically in or around the digestive or urinary system. When describing pain, it emphasizes the intermittent, cramping quality. When describing a baby or animal, it means they are suffering from or prone to colic.

• "She had colicky pain after eating fried food — it came and went in sharp waves."
  • "Their newborn was colicky for the first two months, and they barely slept."
  • "The vet said the horse had been colicky overnight and needed monitoring."
  • "He described a colicky ache in his side, which turned out to be a kidney stone."

In casual, informal speech, people sometimes stretch the word slightly and use colicky to describe any fussy, irritable, difficult-to-please baby or person — even without a clear physical cause. If someone says, "He's been colicky all morning," about a grumpy adult, they are using it loosely to mean irritable or uncomfortable. This is informal usage and not the clinical meaning, but you will encounter it.

Colicky means relating to or suffering from colic — it describes a type of pain that comes in sharp, cramping waves (especially in the abdomen), a baby who cries excessively from apparent digestive discomfort, or an animal (especially a horse) prone to abdominal pain.
3017: To collaborate means to work together with one or more people toward a shared goal, where everyone involved is actively contributing. It's not just being in the same place or on the same team — it means each person genuinely participates, brings their effort or ideas, and helps shape the outcome together.
The key idea behind the word

When people collaborate, no single person is doing everything while others just watch or assist. Everyone has a role. Everyone adds something. The result belongs to all of them together.

Think of it like building a house with a friend. If you lay the bricks while your friend just hands them to you, that's helping. But if you both design the plan, divide the tasks, make decisions together, and build different parts — that's collaborating.
What makes it different from similar words

• Help / assist — One person does the main work; the other supports them. The helper is secondary. In collaboration, no one is secondary.
  • Cooperate — This is more passive. It means not getting in each other's way, following the same rules, working alongside each other. Collaborating is more active — you're building something together, not just working near each other without conflict.
  • Coordinate — This focuses on organizing tasks so people don't clash. Collaboration goes further: it includes sharing ideas, building on each other's thinking, and creating something neither could have made alone.

So collaboration is more than cooperation and more than just helping — it implies joint ownership of the goal and the result.

Collaborate always carries a positive or neutral tone. It suggests mutual respect, equal standing, and shared effort. When you say two people collaborated, you're saying they were partners — not that one was in charge and the other followed orders.

• People: Two scientists collaborated on the research.
  • Teams: The design team and the engineering team collaborated to build the app.
  • Organizations: The two hospitals collaborated to develop a better treatment.
  • Countries: Several nations collaborated on the climate agreement.

The word scales naturally — from two friends working on a small project to entire nations working on a global problem.
How to use it in sentences (grammar patterns)

The most common patterns are:

  • collaborate with (someone) → She collaborated with a photographer on the project.
  • collaborate on (something) → They collaborated on a new album.
  • collaborate to (do something) → The teams collaborated to solve the problem.
  • collaborate with (someone) on (something) → He collaborated with his colleague on the report.

You can also use it without adding anything after it:

  • The departments rarely collaborate.
  • Great results happen when people collaborate.
Examples across different areas of life

• School: Two students write a story together, each contributing ideas and improving the other's writing. → They collaborated on the story.
  • Music: A composer writes the music; a lyricist writes the words. Both shape the final song together. → They collaborated on the song.
  • Medicine: Doctors from five countries pool their findings to develop a vaccine. → They collaborated on the vaccine research.
  • Business: A marketing team and a product team work together to launch a new feature — sharing feedback, adjusting plans, making joint decisions. → They collaborated on the launch.
  • Art: A painter and a sculptor combine their skills to create an installation that uses both mediums. → They collaborated on the artwork.

In some historical contexts (especially from World War II), collaborate was used with a negative meaning — specifically, to mean cooperating with an enemy or occupying force (a collaborator was someone who sided with the oppressors). This usage still exists but is limited to that specific context. In everyday modern use, the word is almost always positive and simply means working together productively.

To collaborate is to join forces with others in a real, active, contributing way — not as a helper, not as a bystander, but as a true partner working toward something shared. The word emphasizes that the effort, the ideas, and ultimately the outcome belong to everyone involved.
3018:
Collaboration is the act of two or more people working together toward a shared goal — where each person contributes their effort, skills, or ideas, and the result is something they build jointly.

The key word is together. Not side by side doing separate things. Not one person doing the work while another watches. But genuinely combined effort, where every participant plays a real role in reaching the outcome.

Think of it this way: if you write an essay alone, that's individual work. If a friend proofreads it afterward, that's still mostly individual work with a little help. But if you and your friend sit down together, discuss ideas, divide sections, challenge each other's thinking, and produce one final essay — that is collaboration. The work belongs to both of you in a real sense.

Collaboration always has three core ingredients:

  • More than one person — it cannot happen alone, by definition.
  • A common goal — everyone is working toward the same outcome, not different ones.
  • Active contribution from each party — everyone brings something to the table: ideas, skills, effort, knowledge, or resources.
What makes collaboration different from similar concepts

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Collaboration vs. Cooperation: Cooperation means people work alongside each other, often on their own separate tasks, to help things go smoothly. Collaboration is deeper — it means people work on the same thing, jointly, with their efforts genuinely intertwined. A class where students share supplies is cooperation. A group project where students plan, create, and present together is collaboration.

Collaboration vs. Assistance: If you help someone carry a heavy box, you're assisting them. The task is still theirs. In collaboration, there is no single "owner" of the task — it belongs to the group.

Collaboration vs. Teamwork: These words are very close and often used interchangeably in everyday language, and that's fine. However, if you want to be precise: teamwork often refers to coordinated effort within assigned roles (each player on a football team has a fixed position), while collaboration tends to emphasize shared thinking and joint problem-solving where roles may be fluid and everyone contributes to the ideas, not just the execution.
Collaboration in different areas of life

The word is used broadly across many fields, and understanding it in different contexts deepens your grasp of it.

In the workplace: When a designer, a writer, and a developer work together to build a website — not just doing their separate jobs, but meeting, discussing, influencing each other's work, and arriving at a unified product — that is collaboration.

In science and research: Scientists from different universities or countries collaborate when they share data, run experiments together, co-author papers, and combine expertise that no single scientist has alone. Great discoveries often come from collaboration across disciplines.

In art and music: When two musicians co-write a song, when filmmakers and composers create a movie together, when artists from different styles produce a joint piece — these are collaborations. The resulting work reflects both their voices.

In education: Students who work on group projects, discuss ideas, and jointly reach conclusions are collaborating. So are teachers who plan lessons together.

In politics and international affairs: When two countries jointly address a problem — like climate change or a disease outbreak — by sharing resources, aligning strategies, and acting together, that too is described as collaboration.

Beyond the literal definition, collaboration carries a spirit of mutual respect and openness. Genuine collaboration requires that participants listen to one another, value each other's input, and be willing to let the final outcome be shaped by everyone — not just the most powerful or loudest person in the room. This is why the word often carries a positive, even idealistic, tone. It suggests equality among contributors and a belief that the result of working together is better than what any one person could have produced alone.

This is sometimes called the idea that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Two people collaborating should produce something neither could have produced alone — that's the promise of collaboration.

Understanding the word also means understanding why it doesn't always go smoothly.

Collaboration requires trust, communication, and willingness to compromise. If people have conflicting goals, refuse to share credit, hoard information, or dominate the process, the collaboration breaks down — even if they're technically "working together." This is why healthy collaboration is often described as a skill, not just an activity. Organizations spend considerable effort building a culture of collaboration, meaning habits and environments where people genuinely work together rather than just appearing to.

Collaboration is not always all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum.

A light collaboration might be two colleagues briefly exchanging ideas that each then develops on their own. A deep collaboration might be two researchers spending years building a theory together, where it's impossible to separate who contributed what. Both are genuinely called collaboration, but they differ in intensity, duration, and how intertwined the contributions are.

• "In collaboration with" — meaning: together with, as a joint effort. ("The book was written in collaboration with a historian.")
  • "Close/tight collaboration" — meaning: intense, ongoing, deeply intertwined joint work.
  • "Foster collaboration" — meaning: to encourage or build conditions where collaboration can happen.
  • "Cross-team / cross-disciplinary collaboration" — collaboration across different departments or fields of expertise, often valued because it brings together people with very different knowledge.
The single-sentence definition, now fully earned

Collaboration is the active, joint effort of two or more people working toward a shared goal — each contributing meaningfully — in a way that the final result is a true product of everyone's combined input, not just one person's work.

Now you have the full picture of this word.
3019:
A collage is a work of art — or any composition — made by taking separate, pre-existing pieces of material and sticking them together onto a flat surface to create one unified whole.

The word names both the process and the finished result. So the thing you make is a collage, and the activity of making it is also called collaging (or making a collage).

The materials used can be almost anything flat enough to be glued down:

  • Cut or torn pieces of newspaper or magazine pages
  • Photographs (printed or cut from magazines)
  • Colored paper, wrapping paper, tissue paper
  • Fabric scraps, ribbons, or thread
  • Receipts, tickets, labels, or other everyday paper items
  • Paint or drawn marks added on top of the pasted pieces

The defining feature is this: you did not create those pieces from scratch. You took things that already existed — a photo, a page from an old book, a scrap of cloth — and arranged them together to make something new. That act of combining ready-made fragments is what makes something a collage.

Think of it like building a picture using puzzle pieces — except you choose the pieces yourself, cut them into whatever shapes you want, and arrange them in any order you like. Usually, the pieces are glued or pasted onto a background (a sheet of paper, a canvas, a board).

Here's what's special: the individual pieces often remain visible and recognizable. If you paste a photograph of a face onto a collage, the viewer can still see it's a photograph. If you paste a strip of newspaper, they can likely read some of the words. The collage doesn't hide its ingredients — it celebrates them.

Because a collage brings together fragments from very different sources, it often creates a feeling of richness, layering, and complexity. Two things that normally have nothing to do with each other — say, a photo of the moon and a piece of floral fabric — can be placed side by side to create a surprising or beautiful effect.

This is one of the reasons collage became so popular in art: it lets you create meaning through contrast and combination, not just through drawing skill.

The word "collage" appears in many areas beyond traditional paper-and-glue art:

In visual art: This is the original and most common use. Artists cut and paste physical materials to make collages. The great Spanish artist Pablo Picasso was among the first to use collage seriously in fine art, in the early 1900s.

In photography (photo collage): Multiple photographs are arranged and combined — either physically printed and stuck together, or digitally on a computer — to make a single image. A photo collage of someone's birthday, for example, might contain 20 different photos arranged in a grid or overlapping pattern.

In digital art: Using software like Photoshop, artists create collages by layering digital images, textures, and graphics. The principle is exactly the same — combining separate elements — just done on a screen instead of a table.

In music: A musical collage is a piece made by blending together sound samples, fragments of other recordings, or very different musical styles. Hip-hop production, for instance, often works like a collage: the producer takes short samples from many old songs and combines them into something new.

In film and video: A video collage (sometimes called a montage) is made by cutting together footage, images, and sounds from different sources to create a new audiovisual experience.

Beyond art, "collage" is often used figuratively to describe anything that is made up of many different, varied pieces coming together:

"The film is a collage of his childhood memories."
"The city's culture is a collage of immigrant traditions."
"Her speech was a collage of quotes, personal stories, and statistics."

In these cases, the speaker means that the thing in question is rich, varied, and assembled from many different sources — just like a real collage. It's not literally made of paper and glue, but the idea of assembling unlike fragments into a whole applies perfectly.
How Collage Differs From Related Things

It helps to know what a collage is not, to sharpen the picture:

  • A painting or drawing is created from scratch using paint, pencil, or ink. A collage uses pre-existing materials. (You can add paint to a collage, though — many collages mix both.)
  • A mosaic is made from small pieces of stone, tile, or glass, usually set into cement or grout. It's related in spirit (combining fragments), but it's three-dimensional and uses hard materials.
  • An assemblage is like a collage, but three-dimensional — objects are arranged and fixed together in space, not just on a flat surface. A collage is essentially a flat assemblage.
  • A montage (especially in film) refers specifically to the technique of editing together a rapid sequence of images or scenes. The words "collage" and "montage" overlap and are sometimes used interchangeably in everyday speech, but "montage" leans more toward film and sequence, while "collage" leans toward visual art and simultaneity.

A collage is a composition — most often a work of art — made by assembling and adhering fragments of pre-existing materials (paper, photos, fabric, etc.) onto a surface to form a new unified whole. The magic of a collage lies in the fact that its parts come from different places and different lives, yet together they create something coherent, surprising, or beautiful. By extension, the word is used in any field — music, film, writing, everyday language — to describe something built from many varied, combined elements.
